dimensions.name: Fairness Evaluation — Discovering Unequal Outcomes
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review whether the product can notice, interpret, and act on unequal outcomes from its own decisions. Focus on whose experience counts as evidence, what aggregate claims can hide, and whether people responsible for outcomes can learn from persistent disparities. This is not a review of isolated data-processing or metric defects.
</scope>

criteria.name: Whose Experience Counts in Evidence
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify product choices that make some people, settings, sources, or ways of participating absent from the evidence used to evaluate learner- or stakeholder-affecting outcomes.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Examine how the product defines its population, selects sources or cases, treats unknowns, and decides what evidence is worthy of evaluation. Ask whose experience becomes invisible or exceptional when these defaults operate as intended.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when repository evidence connects the choice to a consequential claim or decision. Do not infer demographics or demand collection of sensitive attributes without an established product purpose.
</verification>

criteria.name: Categories That Flatten Meaningful Difference
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find product categories or representations that flatten meaningful differences between people, contexts, or experiences before the product evaluates or acts on them.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace how the product names, groups, normalizes, or treats unknown context. Look for a default summary that replaces relevant variation with a single authoritative answer.
</inspect>
<verification>
Require evidence that the omitted distinction changes how people can judge or govern a consequential outcome; a missing schema field or metric alone is not a finding.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unequal Outcomes Without a Learning Loop
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether repeated use can create unequal effects that responsible people have no product-supported way to discover, investigate, or correct.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Follow automated outputs and human approvals over time. Look for missing outcome feedback, inability to compare relevant contexts, or a workflow that records completion while leaving recurring harm invisible.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding needs an evidenced decision or workflow and a credible persistent blind spot. Do not request surveillance, profiling, or universal demographic tracking merely to create a metric.
</verification>

criteria.name: Fairness Evidence That Cannot Inform Action
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify fairness-related evidence that the product creates or relies on but does not make meaningful to the people accountable for a consequential decision.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review who can see evidence, how it is contextualized, whether it reaches the role able to act, and whether uncertainty, exceptions, or affected perspectives are erased on the way.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report a governance gap only when the repository establishes a real decision and a concrete disconnect between evidence and accountable action.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Pedagogy — Defensible Learning Rather Than Convenient Automation
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review how the product defines, represents, and judges learning. Seek assumptions that turn a source, measurable output, or automated default into the authoritative definition of understanding, especially when that choice can persist across learners or classrooms. Do not report ordinary rendering, storage, or workflow defects.
</scope>

criteria.name: Source Material Treated as Neutral Authority
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the product turns a source into assessment or learning authority without a way to recognize perspective, provenance, contestation, or material omissions when those properties matter to the product's domain.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace how sources become questions, recommendations, feedback, or judgments. Look for a design that treats supplied content as neutral ground truth rather than a situated input to a consequential learning decision.
</inspect>
<verification>
Ground the concern in repository evidence of conversion into a learning outcome. Do not presume every source needs multiple viewpoints or that a particular worldview is wrong.
</verification>

criteria.name: Automation Optimized for Answerability Over Learning
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find product defaults that optimize for content easiest to generate, score, compare, or operationalize instead of the learning objective or defensible evidence of understanding the product claims to support.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect what users must specify before generation or judgment, which signals rank outputs, and what the workflow calls success. Consider whether recall, literal matching, or standardization quietly substitutes for reasoning, transfer, uncertainty, or interpretation.
</inspect>
<verification>
A finding requires an evidenced optimization or required workflow that shapes learning judgment. Do not impose a preferred pedagogy that the product context does not support.
</verification>

criteria.name: Learner Understanding Reduced to One Expression
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the product equates understanding with a single answer form, language register, pace, interaction style, or culturally narrow expression despite evidence that its learning decision has broader meaning.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review answer interpretation, feedback, scoring, task design, and permitted alternatives. Ask whether a default representation becomes the only credible way for a learner to demonstrate knowledge.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when the repository shows the representation affects a consequential learning judgment. Do not infer disability, language, or cultural needs that are not evidenced.
</verification>

criteria.name: Learning Judgments Without Meaningful Revision
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify learning or assessment judgments that can become durable without a meaningful route to understand, revisit, or improve the evidence on which they rest.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace feedback, explanations, educator review, learner response, corrections, and later reuse of a judgment. Look for a workflow that treats a generated or automated result as final before affected people can learn from or challenge it.
</inspect>
<verification>
Require evidence that the judgment materially shapes learning, progression, or assessment. A missing convenience feature or transient status display is not enough.
</verification>

criteria.name: Instructional Authority Without Situated Context
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find durable instructional artifacts that are reused as authoritative content without preserving the learning goal, source context, human judgment, or limitations necessary to interpret them responsibly.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Follow generated content, assessments, feedback, and progress evidence across creation, approval, revision, reuse, and later review. Ask whether the product turns situated material into universal instructional authority.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding needs a consequential educational reuse path; loss, corruption, or availability defects alone belong to a conventional engineering review.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Decision Fairness — Justified and Contestable Allocation of Burden
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review consequential product decisions for assumptions that distribute opportunities, restrictions, credibility, or burdens unfairly. Focus on the product's policy and authority relationships, not generic authorization or validation flaws.
</scope>

criteria.name: Consequential Decisions With Unexamined Proxies
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify decision logic that uses a proxy, default category, prior outcome, or convenience signal as if it were justified evidence about a person or situation.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace which inputs influence eligibility, priority, restriction, recommendation, scoring, or access. Consider whether the product silently converts circumstance, access pattern, history, or institutional category into a judgment of merit, risk, or need.
</inspect>
<verification>
A finding needs an evidenced consequential decision and a credible mismatch between what the signal represents and what the decision claims to decide. Do not label every correlation or category as unfair.
</verification>

criteria.name: Policy Defaults That Distribute Burden Unequally
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find product defaults that place the work, delay, risk, or proof burden of a consequential outcome on one role or circumstance without making that allocation deliberate or visible.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review defaults, escalation rules, deadlines, eligibility gates, opt-outs, manual overrides, and recovery routes. Ask who must notice a problem, supply extra evidence, or absorb an automated decision's cost.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only where repository evidence establishes both the default allocation and a material product consequence; unequal effort in an ordinary interface flow is insufficient.
</verification>

criteria.name: One-Way Authority Over Consequential Outcomes
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the product grants an institution, administrator, educator, model, or other powerful role consequential decision authority while denying affected people a meaningful explanation, correction, or contestation path.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace who creates, approves, receives, challenges, and can alter outcomes. Look for an authority structure in which the affected person can only comply with a judgment they cannot inspect or question.
</inspect>
<verification>
Ground the claim in an actual product decision and its stated consequences. Do not require an appeal for non-consequential recommendations or purely informational output.
</verification>

criteria.name: Fairness Claims Without Contestable Governance
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify product claims of fairness, neutrality, mitigation, or responsible automation that cannot be examined or contested by the people accountable for applying them.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review policy configuration, human oversight, exceptions, decision records, and statements that frame an outcome as fair or objective. Ask whether the claim becomes authority without a way to inspect its basis or limits.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding requires a repository-supported fairness claim or governance promise; do not require formal policy machinery where the product makes no such decision.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Inclusion — Whose Circumstances the Product Treats as Normal
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the product's implicit model of a normal user, setting, language, body, culture, resource level, and path to participation. Seek durable exclusion created by defaults and authority—not isolated accessibility, wording, browser, or UI defects.
</scope>

criteria.name: Culturally Narrow or Essentializing Product Models
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify product representations, categories, examples, or decision rules that treat one cultural framing as universal or reduce people to a fixed group identity in a consequential context.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Examine semantic models, generated content constraints, supported interpretations, classification categories, and product language when they govern what counts as correct, safe, capable, or normal.
</inspect>
<verification>
Require a concrete product effect beyond an awkward label or isolated text. Do not infer intent or cultural meaning that repository evidence cannot support.
</verification>

criteria.name: Default User Assumptions That Exclude
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether a consequential workflow assumes a particular level of time, money, technology, connectivity, institutional support, literacy, or prior familiarity as the normal condition for participation.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Follow what the product requires before someone can benefit, recover, give input, or remain eligible. Consider defaults that treat intermittent access, constrained time, or different support structures as failure rather than a legitimate circumstance.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report a finding only when the assumption materially affects access, credibility, opportunity, or burden in an evidenced product flow.
</verification>

criteria.name: Access Needs Treated as Exceptions
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find a product policy that makes a reasonable way of perceiving, communicating, interacting, or demonstrating understanding an exceptional workaround rather than a supported path when it affects a consequential outcome.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review how accommodations, alternative modalities, language choices, assistive workflows, and human support interact with the core decision process. Ask whether the product's central path dismisses or devalues an evidenced alternative.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding needs a domain-relevant product decision and evidence of durable exclusion; a routine visual or control accessibility defect alone is out of scope.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unequally Recoverable Participation
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the product makes participation or recovery from an adverse outcome realistically available only to people with greater time, expertise, authority, or institutional resources.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace what happens after a person is rejected, misunderstood, delayed, or given an unsuitable output. Focus on who bears the work of correction and whether that burden can repeatedly compound.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report a structural participation concern only where the repository links recovery to a consequential opportunity or judgment, not a merely inconvenient workflow.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Transparency — Understandable and Accountable Product Authority
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review whether people can understand what a consequential product output means, why it was produced, what it cannot establish, and how it may be challenged or corrected. Focus on information asymmetry and decision authority, not generic status, error, or loading-state defects.
</scope>

criteria.name: Consequential Logic Hidden From Affected People
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify product decisions that materially affect people while the basis, governing rule, relevant source, or decision-maker remains inaccessible to the people who need to understand it.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace decision inputs, policy, generated output, human approval, and the information each role receives. Ask whether the product's authority depends on a rationale that only an institution or system can see.
</inspect>
<verification>
A finding requires a consequential output and a repository-grounded information asymmetry. Do not require disclosure of secrets, security controls, or irrelevant implementation detail.
</verification>

criteria.name: Claims That Overstate What the System Knows
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether product language, labels, scores, or workflow states present inference, automation, incomplete evidence, or a contested judgment as settled fact or certainty.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review what the product calls correct, complete, fair, safe, ready, predicted, or recommended and compare that claim with the evidence, uncertainty, and role of human judgment represented in the repository.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when overstatement shapes a consequential decision or trust relationship; a minor imprecise label is not enough.
</verification>

criteria.name: Automated Judgments Without Responsible Human Context
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find automated recommendations, classifications, rankings, or judgments that influence a consequential choice without enough contextual explanation for the receiving role to apply responsible human judgment.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace whether the product communicates relevant evidence, limits, alternatives, and uncertainty at the moment someone must act. Consider whether apparent human review is meaningful or merely rubber-stamps an opaque output.
</inspect>
<verification>
Require an evidenced automation-to-decision pathway. Do not require explanatory content for outputs that cannot materially affect a person.
</verification>

criteria.name: Decision Authority Without Recourse
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether an automated or institutional decision can shape a person's opportunity, learning, standing, or treatment while the affected person has no meaningful route to understand, contest, or contextualize it.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Map creation, approval, receipt, explanation, exception, correction, and appeal across roles. Look for a workflow that makes compliance the only available response to an authoritative output.
</inspect>
<verification>
Ground the concern in a real consequential decision; do not demand recourse for informational suggestions or low-stakes automation.
</verification>

criteria.name: Human Review That Cannot Exercise Judgment
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify a nominal human review step that lacks the evidence, time, authority, alternatives, or correction power needed to be meaningful before a consequential automated outcome is used.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace what the reviewer sees, can change, must approve, and learns later. Ask whether review functions as a safeguard or merely shifts responsibility onto a person without decision authority.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when the review is tied to a consequential outcome and repository evidence establishes the gap in meaningful judgment.
</verification>

criteria.name: Missing Provenance and Decision History
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether consequential output can be reused, relied on, or challenged without a meaningful record of its source, revision, human involvement, or governing context.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Follow content, recommendations, and decisions across creation, approval, revision, reuse, and later review. Look for product behavior that converts situated work into an authoritative artifact without preserving the context needed to interpret it.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding needs durable reuse or accountability consequences; lack of an internal audit field or a status message alone is not enough.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Privacy — Purpose, Agency, and Durable Control Over Personal Context
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review how the product uses personal, learner, family, behavioral, or sensitive context as a source of institutional power. Focus on purpose, expectation, role asymmetry, secondary use, and durable control—not generic exposure, logging, authentication, or retention bugs.
</scope>

criteria.name: Collection Without a Stakeholder Purpose
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify data collection or derived personal context that is not meaningfully connected to the product purpose communicated to the people whose information is involved.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace which personal signals become inputs to features or decisions, why they are needed, and whether the product treats availability as permission to use them. Consider inferred data as well as directly supplied data.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when code or product context establishes a real use beyond a defensible purpose; do not treat every stored field as unjustified.
</verification>

criteria.name: Data Use Beyond Reasonable Expectation
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether a product repurposes personal context into a new recommendation, evaluation, ranking, disclosure, or institutional decision that a contributing person has no reasonable way to anticipate or influence.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Follow data from collection through transformations, joins, model or rule inputs, sharing, and decision outputs. Look for a workflow that changes the social meaning of information without making that shift visible.
</inspect>
<verification>
Ground the expectation and new use in repository evidence. Do not infer consent terms, jurisdictional duties, or stakeholder expectations that are not represented.
</verification>

criteria.name: Asymmetric Visibility and Control
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find situations where an institution or privileged role can inspect, combine, or act on personal context while the affected person cannot meaningfully know, correct, limit, or contextualize that use.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review role-based experiences, data-derived decisions, correction routes, notices, and user agency. Ask whether the product creates a one-way observation relationship that shapes a consequential outcome.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding needs an evidenced power imbalance and consequence; absence of a generic privacy setting is not sufficient.
</verification>

criteria.name: Retention That Extends Power Over Time
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether retained personal context, history, or derived labels continue to influence people after the original purpose, accuracy, or relationship has changed.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace reuse of historical signals, profiles, labels, and decision records across time, role changes, corrections, and new contexts. Consider whether old context becomes unchallengeable evidence for later judgment.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when the repository establishes durable influence on a consequential product behavior; an arbitrary storage-duration concern alone is not a finding.
</verification>

dimensions.name: System Integrity — Durable Stakeholder Outcomes and Institutional Accountability
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review whether the product's overall system of roles, automation, handoffs, and recovery preserves accountable, equitable outcomes over time. This dimension is not a catch-all for correctness, security, performance, platform, or UI bugs; it covers systemic product behavior that lets stakeholder harm persist or compound.
</scope>

criteria.name: Product Outcomes Dependent on Invisible Assumptions
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify consequential product outcomes that depend on an unstated institutional, operational, or human assumption that affected people cannot see, assess, or reasonably satisfy.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace handoffs between roles, automated services, policies, and external systems. Ask whether the product presents an outcome as dependable while silently requiring a particular resource, authority, timing, or institutional practice.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report a systemic finding only where the hidden assumption changes stakeholder treatment or accountability. A generic deployment, configuration, or reliability flaw is out of scope.
</verification>

criteria.name: Harmful Patterns That Cannot Be Observed
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the product can repeatedly create a consequential adverse pattern while the people accountable for it lack a product-supported way to recognize the pattern, its source, or its distribution.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review outcome records, role handoffs, aggregation, audit trails, escalation, and repeated automation. Focus on whether the system converts many isolated experiences into invisible institutional drift.
</inspect>
<verification>
Require an evidenced recurring decision or workflow and credible inability to learn from its outcomes. Do not report missing telemetry or monitoring for ordinary operational incidents.
</verification>

criteria.name: Correction and Recovery Burdens That Compound Inequality
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find product behavior that makes correction of a consequential error, unsuitable outcome, or harmful default depend on resources unequally available to affected people or frontline staff.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace recovery, override, support, escalation, documentation, and repeated use. Consider whether an apparently neutral correction path repeatedly transfers cost to the people with least time, authority, expertise, or access.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding needs an evidenced connection to durable stakeholder opportunity, learning, dignity, privacy, or decision fairness; routine error recovery is not enough.
</verification>

criteria.name: Institutional Accountability Gaps in Automated Workflows
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether automation can create a consequential outcome while responsibility for its judgment, correction, and downstream effect is so fragmented that no role can meaningfully own it.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Map creation, approval, deployment, receipt, challenge, and correction across roles and systems. Look for a workflow where each participant can reasonably assume another actor is responsible for an adverse consequence.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when the repository establishes a real automated decision pathway and an accountability gap with material stakeholder consequences.
</verification>

criteria.name: Boundary Decisions That Redefine Who Is Protected
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Identify product boundary rules that determine whose safety, privacy, dignity, or opportunity is protected, and whether those rules silently privilege one role or context over another.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace how the product defines trusted parties, acceptable inputs, escalation, and exceptional cases when those definitions control stakeholder treatment. Focus on policy meaning and power allocation, not exploit mechanics.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding needs an evidenced consequential product boundary and unequal stakeholder consequence; a conventional security vulnerability is out of scope by itself.
</verification>

criteria.name: Scarce Product Capacity Allocated Without Stakeholder Justification
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the product allocates scarce access, time, attention, processing, support, or institutional capacity through defaults that can systematically privilege some stakeholders without a visible, defensible rationale.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Review prioritization, queues, quotas, limits, retries, availability windows, and fallback paths as product rules. Ask who waits, loses access, or receives lower-quality treatment when capacity is constrained.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when repository evidence establishes a consequential allocation rule and a credible unequal burden; generic performance or rate-limit defects are not findings.
</verification>

criteria.name: Adverse Outcomes That Lose Their Institutional Meaning
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Find product behavior that turns a consequential adverse outcome into an isolated, normalized, or unaccountable event, preventing affected people and responsible roles from recognizing what happened or learning from it.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace how the product categorizes, communicates, records, escalates, and later reviews adverse outcomes. Focus on loss of accountability or agency rather than technical exception handling.
</inspect>
<verification>
A valid finding requires an evidenced consequential outcome and a durable governance blind spot; a swallowed error or missing retry is not enough.
</verification>

criteria.name: Conflicting Product Rules Across Roles
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether different product roles, surfaces, or institutional handoffs receive incompatible definitions of a consequential rule, responsibility, entitlement, or outcome.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace policy meaning across interfaces, roles, automated services, documentation, and records. Look for a system in which each participant acts reasonably on a different rule and affected people bear the result.
</inspect>
<verification>
Report only when the conflict changes a stakeholder's real opportunity, treatment, or ability to seek accountability; ordinary contract drift is out of scope.
</verification>
